http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#defi.@value: The consequences of realized risks on natural and human systems, where risks result from the interactions of climate-related hazards (including extreme weather/climate events), exposure, and vulnerability. Impacts generally refer to effects on lives, livelihoods, health and well-being, ecosystems and species, economic, social and cultural assets, services (including ecosystem services), and infrastructure. Impacts may be referred to as consequences or outcomes and can be adverse or beneficial. See also Adaptation, Exposure, Hazard, Vulnerability and Risk.

http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#defi.@value: Climatic impact-driver (CID) Climatic impact-drivers (CIDs) are physical climate system conditions (e.g., means, events, extremes) that affect an element of society or ecosystems. Depending on system tolerance, CIDs and their changes can be detrimental, beneficial, neutral or a mixture of each across interacting system elements and regions. See also Risk, Hazard and Impacts (consequences, outcomes).

dpo:influences(Exp, V) --> 
∃ O, P. Exposure(Exp), Vulnerability(V), PhysicalEndurant(O), ThreatPerdurant(P),

inheresIn(V, O), manifestedBy(V, P) .

dpo:influences(Exp, V) --> Exposure(Exp), Vulnerability(V) .
Indicates that the temporal value is known exactly at its stated resolution.

"Things do not just have value, they have value for someone, and in case their aﬀordances enable certain happenings that positively contribute to the achievement of one's goals. Analogously, things are only at risk from one's perspective, in case their vulnerabilities enable happenings that hurt one's goals."
Sales, T. P., Baião, F., Guizzardi, G., Almeida, J. P. A., Guarino, N., & Mylopoulos, J. (2018, September). The common ontology of value and risk. In International conference on conceptual modeling (pp. 121-135). Cham: Springer International Publishing.

The property is meant to be used to represent the spatial scope of any thing as assessed by an agent (e.g. a municipality, a point of interest), not necessarily corresponding to the exact spatial extension of the phenomenon at the geophysical level.

ElementAtRisk(O) -->
∃ I, P. impactsOn(I, O), dpo:resultOf(I, P),
threatPerdurant(O, P) .

We say that an element is 'at risk' with respect to a certain threat perdurant if it is a service or a physical endurant for which an impact has been documented that results from the same threat perdurant and impacts on that element.
A minimal definition based on temporal precedence only (anything about causality yet).

time:intervalOverlaps(T, T1) .
